note: Lessons for the substantive modules. Exposition of the rules, with the authorities named inline and a `verify` line on every lesson. Where a module has problem questions the lesson hands off to them; where it has none the lesson stands alone and says so, and the reading list is the route onward.

lessons.title: Fundamental liberties, and how a restriction is tested
lessons.summary: Part II rights, the closed list of permitted restrictions in Art 10(2), and the unresolved argument about how hard a court may look.

body.text: Part II of the Federal Constitution contains the fundamental liberties: liberty of the person under Art 5, equality under Art 8, freedom of speech, assembly and association under Art 10, freedom of religion under Art 11, and others. Because Art 4(1) makes the Constitution supreme, these are enforceable against Parliament and not merely aspirations.

What makes constitutional litigation difficult in practice is not finding the right; it is that most of the rights come with an express power to restrict them, and the argument is almost always about the restriction rather than the right.
Article 10(1)(a): every citizen has the right to freedom of speech and expression.

Citizens. Article 10(1) is not a right of everyone within the jurisdiction, unlike Art 5 which speaks of persons. Check your client's status before building an answer on it — it is a one-line point that disposes of an argument entirely.

Article 10(2)(a): Parliament may by law impose on the right conferred by 10(1)(a) such restrictions as it deems necessary or expedient in the interest of the security of the Federation, friendly relations with other countries, public order or morality, and restrictions designed to protect the privileges of Parliament or to provide against contempt of court, defamation, or incitement to any offence.

The list is closed. That is the most important structural fact about the provision, and it gives you an argument that does not depend on any contested standard of review: if a restriction does not fall within one of the named heads, it is not authorised at all, and how deferential the court is prepared to be never arises.

sections.h: The argument that is not settled

body.text: Once a restriction is within a head, how closely may a court examine whether it was necessary? Two lines of authority pull in different directions, and you should know both rather than picking the one you prefer.

PP v Pung Chen Choon: the words “deems necessary or expedient” leave the necessity of a restriction largely to Parliament; the court's role is to ask whether the restriction falls within a permitted head.
body.source: PP v Pung Chen Choon [1994] 1 MLJ 566 (FC)

body.text: Sivarasa Rasiah: fundamental liberties are to be read generously, restrictions must be reasonable, and proportionality is imported through Art 8(1).
body.source: Sivarasa Rasiah v Badan Peguam Malaysia [2010] 2 MLJ 333 (FC)

body.text: Muhammad Hilman is the case where the second approach did real work: the Court of Appeal struck down a statutory restriction on students' political expression as an unreasonable restriction. It shows the reasonableness line is not merely rhetorical.

Do not write that Sivarasa overruled Pung Chen Choon. It did not, and a marker who knows the area will notice. Hold both, argue that the head question is for the court on either view, and put reasonableness as your alternative rather than your only ground.

items: Identify the right and confirm the claimant can hold it — citizen, for Art 10(1).
Identify the restricting law and what exactly it prohibits.
Ask whether the restriction falls within a head permitted by Art 10(2). This is for the court, not for Parliament's own characterisation, or Art 4(1) would have nothing to bite on.
Only then argue reasonableness and proportionality, as the alternative.
Reach a conclusion about validity under Art 4(1) — void to the extent of the inconsistency, not void entirely.

body.text: A statute penalising “any statement likely to cause public disquiet about the conduct of the police” is aimed at a state of public opinion. Public order is about disorder. Naming public order in the long title does not put the provision inside the head, because characterisation is for the court.
The effect of a law matters more than its form. A statute that does not mention a right at all can still restrict it, and the court looks at what the law does rather than at how it is drafted.

No cards yet for this module — the reading list is where the detail lives, and the problem question is the test. It gives you a journalist charged under a fictional provision and a prosecutor arguing that “deems” makes the question one for Parliament. The answer that scores meets that argument directly rather than reciting the right.

quiz.q: Who holds the right in Article 10(1)(a)?
quiz.why: Article 10(1) speaks of citizens, unlike Art 5 which speaks of persons. Check the client's status first.

quiz.q: What does Article 10(2)(a) permit?
options: Parliament to impose restrictions it deems necessary or expedient on stated grounds
The executive to impose any restriction
The courts to define new restrictions
quiz.why: The grounds are a closed list, and whether a restriction falls within a head is for the court.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between Pung Chen Choon and Sivarasa?
options: Both stand; the tension between them is unresolved
quiz.why: Writing that one overruled the other is a mistake a marker who knows the area will notice.

quiz.q: A statute never mentions freedom of speech but in effect restricts it. What follows?
options: The court looks at the effect of the law, not its form
Only the drafter's stated purpose matters
quiz.why: Effect matters more than form, and that is what makes the analysis worth doing.

quiz.q: What is the consequence of inconsistency with the Constitution?
options: The law is void to the extent of the inconsistency
quiz.why: Article 4(1). Severance is the ordinary course.

lessons.title: Homicide: the structure of sections 299 and 300
lessons.summary: Culpable homicide as the genus, murder as the species, and the exceptions that push a case back down.

sections.h: Read the Code, not the common law

body.text: Malaysian criminal law is codified. The Penal Code defines each offence with its own mental element written into the section, and a general common law doctrine of mens rea is not the route to an answer. Your first move in any criminal problem is to find the section and read it.
Homicide is the best illustration, because the structure is unusually clean once you see it and completely opaque if you approach it with English categories.
Section 299 defines culpable homicide. Section 300 tells you when culpable homicide is murder. The exceptions to s 300 tell you when it drops back. Three steps, always in that order.

Section 299: culpable homicide is causing death by an act done with the intention of causing death, or with the intention of causing such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, or with the knowledge that the act is likely to cause death.

Culpable homicide is the genus. Murder is a species of it. So you never ask “is this murder or culpable homicide” as though they were alternatives — you ask whether it is culpable homicide, and then whether it is the kind that s 300 makes murder.
Section 300 has four limbs, lettered (a) to (d). Any one of them turns culpable homicide into murder.

items: (a) the act is done with the intention of causing death;
(b) with the intention of causing bodily injury the offender knows to be likely to cause the death of the person harmed;
(c) with the intention of causing bodily injury, and the injury intended is sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death;

(d) with knowledge that the act is so imminently dangerous that it must in all probability cause death or such bodily injury as is likely to cause death, and without any excuse for incurring the risk.

body.text: Section 300(c) is two questions: did the accused intend to inflict the injury actually inflicted, and is that injury objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death.
body.source: Penal Code, s 300(c); PP v Visuvanathan [1978] 1 MLJ 159, applying Virsa Singh

body.text: Limb (c) is the one the prosecution reaches for most often, because the second question is objective and answered by the pathologist rather than by anything in the accused's head. That the accused did not realise the blow could kill is simply not the question.

Students reflexively run limb (a) because someone died. On a single blow with something picked up in the moment, (a) is hard and (c) is straightforward. Choosing the wrong limb is choosing a harder case than the prosecution has to prove.

If a limb of s 300 is made out, the offence is murder unless an exception applies. The exceptions do not acquit — they reduce murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder. That is the single most common error in a homicide answer: treating provocation as a defence rather than as a reduction.
Exception 1: culpable homicide is not murder if the offender, whilst deprived of the power of self-control by grave and sudden provocation, causes the death of the person who gave the provocation.

Both adjectives have to be satisfied and they fail in different ways. Grave asks how serious the provocation was; sudden asks whether there was time for passion to cool. A long-brewing grievance may be grave and is unlikely to be sudden.

The Explanation makes whether the provocation was grave and sudden a question of fact, which is what allows words alone to amount to provocation. There are three provisos: the provocation must not have been sought or voluntarily provoked by the offender, nor given by anything done in obedience to the law or by a public servant acting lawfully, nor by anything done in the lawful exercise of the right of private defence.

Exception 4 covers a sudden fight in the heat of passion upon a sudden quarrel, without the offender taking undue advantage or acting in a cruel or unusual manner. It is worth checking on any facts involving a scuffle.

Section 302 punishes murder; section 304 punishes culpable homicide not amounting to murder, and it splits by mental element — the intention limb and the knowledge limb carry different maxima, so your finding on which limb was satisfied determines which applies.

The mandatory death penalty for murder was abolished in 2023 and sentencing is now discretionary. Do not state the range from memory or from an older textbook; read the current provision. This is the single most likely thing on this page to have moved since it was written.

Work the problem question, which gives you a single blow, an unambiguous pathologist, and a provocation that is arguably grave and doubtfully sudden. The marks are in taking s 300(c) in its two separate parts and then arguing both sides of suddenness rather than asserting one.

quiz.q: What is the relationship between ss 299 and 300?
options: Culpable homicide is the genus; murder is the species
They are alternative offences of equal rank
Section 300 defines the sentence for s 299
Section 299 applies only where s 300 does not
quiz.why: Every murder is culpable homicide; not every culpable homicide is murder.

quiz.q: Section 300(c) asks two questions. What are they?
options: Did the accused intend the injury actually inflicted, and is that injury objectively sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death
Did the accused intend death, and was death caused
Was the act imminently dangerous, and did the accused know it
Was there provocation, and was it grave and sudden
quiz.why: The second limb is objective, which is why (c) is often easier to make out than (a).

quiz.q: A single blow is struck with an object picked up in the moment and the victim dies. Which limb is the natural one to run?
quiz.why: Students reflexively run (a) because someone died; on these facts intention to cause death is hard and (c) is straightforward.

quiz.q: What does Exception 1 to s 300 require?
options: Grave and sudden provocation depriving the offender of self-control, and death of the person who gave it
quiz.why: The exception reduces murder to culpable homicide not amounting to murder.

quiz.q: What should you not state from memory about the sentence for murder?
options: The range — the mandatory death penalty was abolished in 2023 and sentencing is discretionary
quiz.why: Sentencing provisions move. Check a current source.

lessons.title: Property offences: how possession was obtained
lessons.summary: Theft, criminal breach of trust and cheating are separated by one question, and it is not what was taken.

body.text: Three offences cover most dishonest dealings with property, and students routinely charge all of them as theft because the accused ended up with something they were not entitled to. That is the wrong question. The right one is how the accused came to have the property in the first place.

items: Taken out of another's possession without consent → theft.
Received lawfully, then misappropriated → criminal breach of trust.
Obtained by consent, where the consent was procured by deception → cheating.

body.text: Ownership is not the test. In all three the property belongs to someone else; that is what makes each of them an offence. Possession and consent are what separate them.
Section 378: whoever, intending to take dishonestly any movable property out of the possession of any person without that person's consent, moves that property in order to such taking, commits theft.

Two elements do the work: the property must be taken out of another's possession, and it must be without consent. Note also that only movable property can be stolen, and that the offence is complete on moving the property — it is not necessary that the accused get away with it.

Section 405: whoever, being in any manner entrusted with property, or with any dominion over property, dishonestly misappropriates or converts it to his own use, or dishonestly uses or disposes of it in violation of any direction of law or legal contract, commits criminal breach of trust.
Here the accused begins with the property lawfully. There is no taking out of anyone's possession because they already had it. The wrong is the misappropriation of something entrusted.
Where the accused is a clerk or servant, an aggravated form applies with a heavier penalty, and it is the form that fits most employee cases.

A cashier authorised to take payment from customers receives RM200 and pockets it, recording no sale. She had the money lawfully in her capacity as cashier, so this is criminal breach of trust and not theft. If instead she takes a drill from the display shelf on her way out, that is theft — the stock was in the shop's possession and she was never entrusted with it. Being a cashier does not put the whole shop in her hands.

Whether an employee has possession or mere custody of what passes through their hands is a genuine question, and the answer depends on the scope of what they were entrusted with. Argue it rather than asserting it.
Section 415: whoever, by deceiving any person, fraudulently or dishonestly induces the person so deceived to deliver any property to any person, commits cheating.
Cheating is the odd one out, because the victim consents. They hand the property over willingly. What vitiates the consent is the deception that produced it, and that is the element to establish.

Where the deception induces delivery of property, the punishment section is s 420 rather than the general one — a distinction worth getting right, because charging under the wrong punishment section is a real error rather than a stylistic one.

sections.h: Working a mixed set of facts

body.text: Problem questions in this area typically give you three or four incidents in a single narrative and invite you to label them all the same way. Take each incident separately and ask the organising question of each. The examiner is testing whether you can distinguish, not whether you can recite three definitions.

Do not forget that the same facts can support more than one charge, and that alternative charges are ordinary practice. Saying which is the better charge and why is worth more than picking one and moving on.

The problem question gives you a cashier and three incidents on one Saturday, with an investigating officer who proposes to charge all three as theft. Only one of them is. The marks are in the reason, stated in a line: how the accused came to have the property.

quiz.q: What single question separates theft, criminal breach of trust and cheating?
quiz.why: Taken without consent; received lawfully then misappropriated; obtained by consent procured by deception.

quiz.q: Property is received lawfully and then misappropriated. Which offence?
quiz.why: Section 405: entrusted with property or dominion over it, then dishonest misappropriation.

quiz.q: Which section defines theft?
quiz.why: Dishonest taking of movable property out of another's possession without consent, with a moving of the property.

quiz.q: Consent to part with property is obtained by deception. Which offence?
quiz.why: Section 415: inducing delivery by deceiving the person.

quiz.q: Can one set of facts support more than one charge?

No, the charges are mutually exclusive
quiz.why: Saying which is the better charge, and why, is part of the answer.

lessons.title: Formation: the moment a contract exists
lessons.summary: Section 4 fixes different moments for different communications, and section 5 decides the race between acceptance and revocation.

sections.h: A statute, not the common law

body.text: Malaysian contract law is statutory. The Contracts Act 1950 codifies formation, and it does not always match the English rules that a common law textbook will give you. Reading English contract law across without checking the Act is the most reliable way to get a Malaysian contract answer wrong.
Formation is the clearest case, because the Act codifies the postal rule in a form that produces results the English cases do not.
Section 2(a): when one person signifies to another his willingness to do or to abstain from doing anything, with a view to obtaining the assent of that other, he is said to make a proposal.
The Act says proposal where an English text says offer, and promise where it says acceptance. The concepts are the same; the vocabulary should follow the statute you are working in.

A proposal must be distinguished from an invitation to treat — a display of goods, an advertisement, an auction notice — which invites proposals rather than making one. That distinction is common law and carries over.

This is the section that decides most formation problems, and the thing to notice is that it fixes different moments depending on which communication it is and which party it is being used against. There is no single rule to apply.
Section 4(1): communication of a proposal is complete when it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made.

Section 4(2): communication of an acceptance is complete — (a) as against the proposer, when it is put in a course of transmission to him, so as to be out of the power of the acceptor; and (b) as against the acceptor, when it comes to the knowledge of the proposer.

Section 4(3): communication of a revocation is complete — (a) as against the person who makes it, when it is put into a course of transmission; and (b) as against the person to whom it is made, when it comes to his knowledge.

Read those three together and the pattern appears. Posting is enough to bind the person the communication is aimed at only in one case: acceptance, as against the proposer. Everywhere else the section requires knowledge. That asymmetry is deliberate and it is where the marks are.
Section 5(1): a proposal may be revoked at any time before the communication of its acceptance is complete as against the proposer, but not afterwards.

Combine s 5(1) with s 4(2)(a) and the deadline is precise: the proposer may revoke until the moment the acceptance is posted, and not after. Combine it with s 4(3)(b) and the revocation only reaches the acceptor when the acceptor knows of it.

An offer is posted on 3 March. The offeror posts a revocation on 10 March, delivered to the offeree's office on 12 March in the afternoon but unread until 14 March. The offeree posts an acceptance at 9am on 12 March. The acceptance was complete against the proposer when posted, at 9am on 12 March. The revocation was complete against the offeree only on 14 March, when he read it. The revocation is too late and there is a contract.
Delivery is not knowledge. Section 4(3)(b) says knowledge, and a letter sitting unopened on a desk has not been communicated. This is the step most answers skip.

Section 6 sets out the modes of revocation: notice, lapse of time, failure to fulfil a condition precedent, and the death or mental disorder of the proposer where that fact is known to the acceptor before acceptance.
A proposal stated to be open until a date is not thereby irrevocable. A promise to keep an offer open is itself a promise, and without consideration it does not bind.
A promise to keep an offer open for a stated period is not binding unless supported by consideration; the proposer may revoke within the period.
body.source: Macon Works & Trading Sdn Bhd v Phang Hon Chin [1976] 2 MLJ 177

body.text: Students who spot this often over-apply it. It means the offeror could have revoked in time — not that they did. Check the timing under ss 4 and 5 before concluding either way.

The problem question is two letters crossing in the post, with both parties advancing an argument that is wrong. Working it properly means applying a different subsection to each communication rather than reaching for one rule and using it everywhere.

quiz.q: When is communication of a proposal complete?
options: When it comes to the knowledge of the person to whom it is made
quiz.why: Section 4(1). Each kind of communication has its own moment.

quiz.q: When is communication of an acceptance complete as against the proposer?
options: When it is put in a course of transmission, out of the acceptor's power
When the acceptor decides to accept
quiz.why: Section 4(2)(a). As against the acceptor it is complete when it comes to the proposer's knowledge.

quiz.q: Until when may a proposal be revoked?
options: Until communication of the acceptance is complete as against the proposer
quiz.why: Section 5(1) — which is why the moment fixed by s 4(2)(a) decides the race.

quiz.q: A revocation letter sits unopened on the offeree's desk. Has it been communicated to him?
options: Only if sent by registered post
quiz.why: Delivery is not knowledge, and this is the step most answers get wrong.

quiz.q: A proposer promises to keep an offer open for fourteen days. Is that binding?
options: Yes, if the offeree relied on it
quiz.why: It means the proposer could have revoked in time — not that they did. Check the timing under ss 4 and 5 first.

lessons.title: Consideration under a statute, not the common law
lessons.summary: Section 2(d) differs from English law in two ways that decide cases, and section 26 saves three promises that would otherwise fail.

body.text: Consideration is the topic where importing English law does the most damage, because the English rules are famous and the Malaysian definition is statutory and different. Two of the differences are decisive on ordinary facts, and both appear in a single sentence of the Act.

Section 2(d): when, at the desire of the promisor, the promisee or any other person has done or abstained from doing, or does or abstains from doing, or promises to do or to abstain from doing, something, such act or abstinence or promise is called a consideration for the promise.
Read the sentence twice and two phrases should stand out.

items: “has done or abstained from doing” — a past act counts. English law's rule that past consideration is no consideration does not apply here.
“the promisee or any other person” — consideration need not move from the promisee. It may come from a stranger to the promise.

body.text: Kepong Prospecting is the authority usually cited for the first, the Privy Council having treated services rendered before the agreement as good consideration under s 2(d).
Past consideration is good consideration in Malaysia, and consideration need not move from the promisee.
body.source: Contracts Act 1950, s 2(d); Kepong Prospecting Ltd v Schmidt [1968] 1 MLJ 170 (PC)

body.text: The second point does not abolish privity. Consideration may come from a stranger; a stranger to the contract still cannot sue on it. Keep the two rules apart — they are often confused, and Kepong Prospecting is cited for both.

The words “at the desire of the promisor” remain a real requirement. An act done spontaneously, that nobody asked for, is not obviously consideration even though it is past — which is where s 26 becomes the safer argument.

Section 26: an agreement made without consideration is void, unless — (a) it is in writing and registered, and made on account of natural love and affection between parties standing in a near relation to each other; (b) it is a promise to compensate, wholly or in part, a person who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor; or (c) it is a promise, in writing and signed by the person to be charged, to pay wholly or in part a debt of which the creditor might have enforced payment but for the law of limitation.
Each exception has its own formality, and the formality is usually what decides the case rather than the substance.

items: (a) needs writing AND registration. Writing alone is not enough, and this is the limb students most often fail to state fully.
(b) needs the earlier act to have been voluntary and done for the promisor. This is the safe route for the spontaneous good turn that s 2(d) leaves doubtful.
(c) needs writing signed by the person to be charged, and a debt that is time-barred rather than merely unpaid.

body.text: A neighbour returns a lost dog unasked; a week later the owner signs a note promising RM500. Section 2(d) arguably covers it as past consideration, but “at the desire of the promisor” is awkward because nobody asked. Section 26(b) covers it squarely — a promise to compensate someone who has already voluntarily done something for the promisor. Plead (b) first.

A father promises RM20,000 orally, out of natural love and affection, when his daughter finishes her degree. Near relation, plainly. Natural love and affection, expressly. But nothing was written and nothing was registered, so s 26(a) is not satisfied and the promise is void.
Failing that second example on intention to create legal relations is the wrong answer with the right outcome. The Act gives you a formality; use it. Marks go to the provision, not to the conclusion.

Explanation 2 to s 26: an agreement is not void merely because the consideration is inadequate, but inadequacy may be taken into account in determining whether the promisor's consent was freely given.

This codifies the familiar rule that the courts do not police the bargain, with the familiar qualification that a grossly one-sided bargain is evidence of something having gone wrong in the making of it.

The problem question gives you three promises and a junior who has advised that all three fail, on grounds taken straight from an English textbook. Two of the three succeed. The exercise is noticing which of the junior's propositions is English law that the Act displaces.

options: Past consideration is good, and consideration need not move from the promisee
Consideration must move from the promisee only
quiz.why: Both differences decide cases, and both come straight from the words of the section.

quiz.q: Does s 2(d) abolish privity?
options: No — a stranger to the contract still cannot sue on it
Only where consideration moved from the stranger

quiz.q: What does s 26(a) require?
options: Writing and registration, natural love and affection, and parties in a near relation
quiz.why: Writing alone is not enough, and this is the limb most often stated incompletely.

options: Inadequacy of consideration does not make an agreement void, but may bear on free consent
Adequacy is for the parties alone
quiz.why: It is a bridge between consideration and the free consent provisions.

quiz.q: A promise is made in return for a past voluntary act done for the promisor. Which limb saves it?
quiz.why: The act must have been voluntary and done for the promisor.

lessons.title: From arrest to charge
lessons.summary: How the Criminal Procedure Code classifies offences, and what that classification decides about arrest, remand and bail.

body.text: Criminal procedure looks like a mass of detail until you notice that a small number of classifications in the First Schedule to the Criminal Procedure Code drive most of it. Whether the police may arrest without a warrant, whether they may investigate without an order, and whether bail is available are all answered by looking the offence up rather than by reasoning about it.
The First Schedule to the CPC classifies each offence as seizable or non-seizable, and as bailable, non-bailable or unbailable. Look the offence up before reasoning about the procedure.

Malaysia says seizable where England says arrestable. Using the English vocabulary signals you are working from an English textbook, and the underlying classification is not identical, so it is not merely a naming difference.

For a seizable offence a police officer may arrest without a warrant. For a non-seizable offence the general position is that a warrant or an order is required. But the powers sit under constitutional guarantees that apply whatever the classification, and those are where the arguments usually are.
Article 5(3): a person arrested shall be informed as soon as may be of the grounds of his arrest and shall be allowed to consult and be defended by a legal practitioner of his choice.

Article 5(4): a person arrested and not released shall without unreasonable delay, and in any case within twenty-four hours, be produced before a magistrate and shall not be further detained without the magistrate's authority.

The twenty-four hours excludes the time necessary for the journey to the magistrate. Further detention requires a remand order, and the magistrate is deciding whether continued detention is justified for the investigation rather than rubber-stamping the request.

The right to counsel under Art 5(3) is not always given effect at the moment of arrest, and the case law on when access must be allowed is worth reading in full rather than summarised. This is a live and contested area.
Bail in Malaysia is largely a matter of classification rather than of general judicial discretion, which is a real difference from the English approach a common law textbook will describe.

items: Bailable — bail is available as of right.
Non-bailable — bail is at the court's discretion.
Unbailable — bail is not available at all.

body.text: So the first question is never whether bail should be granted. It is which of the three categories the offence falls into, and that is answered from the Schedule.

Special legislation frequently displaces the ordinary rules, and security and drugs legislation in particular has its own bail provisions. Check whether the charge is under the Penal Code or under a specific Act before applying the general position.

Investigation into a seizable offence may proceed without an order; a non-seizable offence generally requires one. The investigation produces the investigation papers, which go to the Deputy Public Prosecutor, and the decision to prosecute is the Public Prosecutor's.
The charge must state the offence, and enough particulars of time, place, and the person or thing concerned, to give the accused notice of what he is charged with.

A defective charge is not automatically fatal — the question is usually whether the accused was prejudiced or misled — but the drafting rules exist because a person cannot answer a case they have not been told.

sections.h: The trial, and the standard at the close of the prosecution case

body.text: At the close of the prosecution case the court asks whether a prima facie case has been made out. If it has, the accused is called upon to enter his defence; if not, he is acquitted.
A prima facie case requires the court to undertake a maximum evaluation of the prosecution evidence — to test its credibility — and to ask whether, if unrebutted, it would warrant a conviction.

That standard matters because a minimum evaluation, which merely asks whether there is some evidence on each element, would put an accused to his defence on evidence no reasonable court could convict on. The point is regularly argued and worth understanding rather than reciting.

If the defence is called, the accused may give sworn evidence, make an unsworn statement from the dock, or remain silent, and the consequences of each differ. Conviction still requires proof beyond reasonable doubt on the whole of the evidence.

The most useful thing you can do is read the First Schedule itself — not a summary of it — and follow one offence through: its classification, the arrest power it gives, and the bail position that follows. The structure becomes obvious once you have done it once.

lessons.title: Negligence, in four questions
lessons.summary: Duty, breach, causation and remoteness — and the two places where Malaysian law has taken its own line.

body.text: Almost every negligence problem is answered by four questions in order, and answering them out of order is the commonest way to write a poor answer. Establish each before moving to the next, and say which one the case actually turns on.

items: Duty — did the defendant owe this claimant a duty of care?
Breach — did the defendant fall below the standard required?
Causation — did the breach cause the damage, in fact and in law?
Remoteness — was the damage of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable?

body.text: Damage is required. Negligence is not actionable per se: no loss, no claim, however careless the conduct.

Where the situation is an established one — road users, doctor and patient, employer and employee — a duty exists and the point should be dealt with in a sentence. The three-stage analysis is for novel situations, and using it on a car accident wastes the time you needed for causation.
The three-stage test: reasonable foreseeability of harm, a relationship of proximity between the parties, and whether it is fair, just and reasonable to impose a duty.
body.source: Caparo, adopted in Malaysia in Majlis Perbandaran Ampang Jaya v Steven Phoa Cheng Loon [2006] 2 MLJ 389 (FC)

body.text: Ampang Jaya is the Malaysian authority to cite, and it is worth reading rather than citing second-hand, because it also engages the difficult question of a public authority's liability. Lok Kok Beng later revisited the approach and is the other case to know.

Pure economic loss and psychiatric injury have their own restrictive rules and are not simply harder instances of ordinary duty. Identify them as separate categories rather than running the three-stage test and hoping.

The standard is objective: what a reasonable person would have done in the defendant's position. The defendant's own inexperience does not lower it, and the standard for a professional is that of the reasonably competent member of that profession.

Whether the standard was met is judged by weighing the likelihood of harm, the seriousness of the harm if it occurs, the cost and practicability of precautions, and the social utility of the activity. Those factors are how you argue breach rather than assert it.

On a doctor's duty to advise of risks, Malaysia has departed from the Bolam test and adopted the approach in Rogers v Whitaker: the question is what a reasonable patient would want to know, not what a responsible body of medical opinion would disclose.
body.source: Foo Fio Na v Dr Soo Fook Mun [2007] 1 MLJ 593 (FC)

body.text: This is the first of the two places where an English textbook will mislead you. Foo Fio Na is a genuine Malaysian departure and a marker will expect you to know it. Note carefully what it decided about — advice and disclosure of risk — and be careful before extending it to diagnosis and treatment.
Factual causation is the but-for test: would the damage have occurred but for the breach? If it would have happened anyway, the breach caused nothing, however negligent it was.

Legal causation asks whether anything broke the chain — a novus actus interveniens, whether an act of the claimant, a third party, or a natural event. The question is whether the intervening act was so unreasonable or unforeseeable that it displaces the defendant's responsibility.

A doctor negligently fails to examine a patient who was already dying of a poison for which there was no treatment. The failure is a breach. It caused nothing, because the patient would have died regardless — the claim fails at causation, not at breach.
Damage is too remote unless it is of a kind that was reasonably foreseeable. The precise manner of its occurrence and its extent need not be.
body.source: The Wagon Mound; standard common law

body.text: Two doctrines then reduce or defeat what is recovered. Contributory negligence apportions the damages where the claimant's own carelessness contributed to the harm; it is a reduction rather than a defence, and in Malaysia it is statutory.
Contributory negligence: damages are reduced to such extent as the court thinks just and equitable having regard to the claimant's share in the responsibility.
Volenti non fit injuria — voluntary assumption of risk — is a complete defence and is correspondingly rare, requiring genuine knowledge of the risk and genuine consent to it.

Watch the limitation period. A tort claim is generally barred six years after the cause of action accrued, and in negligence the cause of action accrues when damage occurs rather than when the careless act was committed.

lessons.title: Title by registration, and the limits of indefeasibility
lessons.summary: The Torrens system, section 340, and the case that had to be overruled to make it work as intended.

body.text: Malaysian land law is a Torrens system, and the single idea that organises it is that the register is not evidence of title — it is the title. A person becomes the proprietor by being registered, not by having a good chain of documents that registration then records.
Title by registration, not registration of title. The register is conclusive, and a purchaser deals with the register rather than investigating the history behind it.
body.source: National Land Code; the Torrens principle

body.text: The point of the system is to make conveyancing safe and cheap by removing the need to trace a chain of deeds back through decades. Everything difficult in the subject comes from the cases where that promise collides with a genuine victim of fraud or forgery.

Section 6 of the Civil Law Act 1956 excludes English land law, and this is why. Importing English doctrines of equitable interests and notice would cut across the register's conclusiveness, which is the whole mechanism.
Section 340(1): the title or interest of any person for the time being registered as proprietor, or in whose name any lease, charge or easement is registered, is indefeasible.

That is the promise. Subsection (2) is the set of exceptions, and it is short and exhaustive — indefeasibility is defeated where the registration was obtained by fraud or misrepresentation to which the proprietor was a party or privy, or by forgery or by an insufficient or void instrument, or where the title was unlawfully acquired in purported exercise of a power conferred by written law.

Then comes the proviso, which is the provision the whole subject turns on. Where a title is liable to be set aside under subsection (2), it is nevertheless protected in the hands of a purchaser in good faith and for valuable consideration.

Deferred indefeasibility: the immediate registered proprietor whose registration was procured by fraud or forgery takes a defeasible title. A subsequent bona fide purchaser for value takes an indefeasible one.
body.source: National Land Code, s 340(2) and the proviso to s 340(3)

body.text: So the forger's transferee can be unwound; the innocent person who then buys from that transferee cannot. The system draws the line one transaction later than a naive reading suggests, and the reason is that the innocent purchaser is the person the register exists to protect.

sections.h: The case that had to be overruled

body.text: This is the best example in Malaysian law of the precedent doctrine doing real work, and it is worth knowing as a piece of legal history as well as for the rule.

In Adorna Properties the Federal Court read s 340 as conferring immediate indefeasibility — so that even the immediate transferee under a forged instrument obtained a good title. The consequence was that a registered proprietor could lose their land to a forger's purchaser with no remedy, which inverted the protective purpose of the exceptions.
Tan Ying Hong overruled Adorna Properties and restored deferred indefeasibility: a registration obtained by forgery is defeasible in the hands of the immediate transferee.
body.source: Tan Ying Hong v Tan Sian San [2010] 2 MLJ 1 (FC)

body.text: Textbooks and judgments predating 2010 may state the Adorna position. Check the date of anything you read on indefeasibility, and note that the intervening years produced decisions applying a rule that is no longer good law.

The Code provides a closed set of registrable dealings — transfer, lease, charge, easement — and the vocabulary is not the English one. Land is charged, not mortgaged, and the chargee's remedies are statutory: an order for sale, or possession, on the terms the Code lays down.

A caveat is the mechanism for protecting an unregistered claim. It does not create an interest; it prevents dealings from being registered while it stands, which buys the caveator time to establish the claim in court. Private, registrar's, lien-holder's and trust caveats each have their own conditions.
A caveat entered without a caveatable interest exposes the caveator to compensation. It is not a free way to obstruct a transaction.

No cards or problems for this module yet. Read s 340 itself, slowly, including the proviso — it is a short provision that repays being read five times — and then read Tan Ying Hong to see what the Federal Court thought had gone wrong.

lessons.title: The company as a person, and the duties that follow
lessons.summary: Separate legal personality, when the courts look behind it, and what the Companies Act 2016 requires of directors.

sections.h: One idea, and everything else follows

body.text: Company law rests on a single proposition that is stranger than it looks: a company incorporated under the Act is a legal person distinct from the people who own and run it. It can own property, contract, sue and be sued in its own name, and it continues to exist as members come and go.
A company is a body corporate with legal personality separate from its members. Its members are not, by reason only of membership, liable for its obligations.
body.source: Salomon v A Salomon & Co Ltd [1897] AC 22; Companies Act 2016

body.text: Salomon is the case, and it matters because the House of Lords upheld the separateness even where one man owned almost all the shares, ran the business, and was also its secured creditor. The company was not his agent and not a sham; it was a different person.
Limited liability is a consequence rather than the principle. Because the company owes the debts, the member's exposure is limited to what remains unpaid on their shares.

The courts will occasionally look behind the separate personality and treat the company and its controllers as one. The circumstances are narrower than students expect, and asserting that the veil should be lifted because a result seems unfair is not an argument.

items: Statute — where an Act expressly imposes liability on directors or members, which is by far the commonest route.
Fraud or evasion — where the corporate form is used to evade an existing legal obligation or to conceal wrongdoing.
Agency — where the company is genuinely acting as agent for its controller on ordinary agency principles, rather than merely being controlled by them.

body.text: Control alone is never enough. A wholly owned subsidiary is a separate person from its parent, and a one-member company is a separate person from its member — that is precisely what Salomon decided. An answer that lifts the veil because the defendant owned all the shares has not identified a ground.
The Companies Act 2016 replaced the 1965 Act and made structural changes that older textbooks will not reflect. Three are worth knowing before you read anything on the subject.

items: The memorandum and articles of association were replaced by a single optional constitution. A company may have none, in which case the Act supplies its internal rules.
A private company may be formed and run with a single member and a single director.
The authorised capital concept and the par value of shares were abolished — shares are issued without nominal value.

body.text: This is the module where an out-of-date text does the most damage. If a book refers to the memorandum and articles or to authorised capital as current law, it predates 2016 and should be treated as history.
The Act states the core duties, and they sit alongside rather than replacing the equitable and common law duties that developed before them.
A director shall at all times exercise his powers in accordance with the Act, for a proper purpose and in good faith in the best interest of the company.

A director shall exercise reasonable care, skill and diligence with the knowledge, skill and experience which may reasonably be expected of a director having the same responsibilities, and any additional knowledge, skill and experience which the director in fact has.

Notice the shape of the second duty: an objective floor set by the office, raised for a particular director by whatever additional expertise they actually possess. An accountant on the board is held to more than the minimum, and a director who takes no interest in the company's affairs is not held to less.

Two further points recur. The duty in s 213(1) is owed to the company, not to individual shareholders and not to creditors in the ordinary case — which is what makes the question of who may sue on a breach a subject of its own. And a director must not use their position or the company's property, information or opportunity to gain a benefit for themselves or cause detriment to the company.

A director learns, in board discussions, of a contract the company is pursuing, and takes it personally. That the company might have failed to win it is not usually an answer: the objection is to the use of the position and the information, not to the loss.

Because the duty is owed to the company, the company is the proper claimant when it is breached. That is the source of the rule that an individual member cannot ordinarily sue for a wrong done to the company, and of the statutory routes that exist around it — the derivative action brought with leave on the company's behalf, and the oppression remedy where the affairs of the company are conducted in a manner oppressive to a member.
Keep the two apart. A derivative action vindicates the company's right; an oppression claim vindicates the member's own. Confusing them is a standard way to answer the wrong question.

lessons.title: Relevancy is the gate
lessons.summary: The Evidence Act is a closed list of what may be proved, which is a different system from the English law of admissibility.

sections.h: Why an English textbook will mislead you here

body.text: The Evidence Act 1950 descends from the Indian Evidence Act of 1872, drafted by Stephen, and it is a code. It does not restate the English law of evidence and it is not organised the way English evidence is organised.

The English approach asks whether a piece of evidence is admissible, starting from a general principle that relevant evidence is admissible unless an exclusionary rule bites. The Act inverts this. It sets out, in Part I, the categories of fact that are relevant, and nothing outside those categories may be proved at all.
Evidence may be given of facts in issue and of such other facts as are declared relevant by the Act, and of no others.

So the question is never simply “is this relevant?” in the ordinary sense. It is “which section makes this relevant?” If you cannot name one, the evidence does not come in — and an answer that argues relevance without a section has missed the structure of the whole Act.
Part I runs through the categories. You do not need them all at once, but you should know the shape and be able to find the right one.

items: Facts forming part of the same transaction — the res gestae provision.
Facts which are the occasion, cause or effect of facts in issue.
Motive, preparation, and previous or subsequent conduct.
Facts necessary to explain or introduce a relevant fact.
Admissions, and confessions as a special class of admission.
Statements by persons who cannot be called as witnesses — the principal exceptions to the exclusion of hearsay.
Opinions of experts, on points of science, art, foreign law, handwriting or fingerprints.
Character, which is relevant in narrow and different circumstances in civil and criminal cases.

body.text: Hearsay is worth a note because the Act handles it differently from English law. There is no single hearsay rule with a list of exceptions; rather, statements by absent persons are simply not made relevant except where a section makes them so — which produces similar results by a different route.
Part II deals with proof, and the burden provisions are the ones you will use most often.
Whoever desires any court to give judgment as to any legal right or liability, dependent on the existence of facts which he asserts, must prove that those facts exist.
The burden of proof in a suit or proceeding lies on that person who would fail if no evidence at all were given on either side.

Section 103 puts the burden as to any particular fact on the person who wishes the court to believe in its existence, and s 106 places on a person the burden of proving a fact especially within their own knowledge. That last one recurs constantly in criminal cases and is regularly over-argued by prosecutors.

Distinguish the legal burden, which does not shift, from the evidential burden, which does. Saying that the burden shifts to the accused, without saying which burden, is the standard error and it matters — the legal burden in a criminal case stays with the prosecution throughout.
The Act distinguishes facts the court shall presume from facts it may presume. The discretionary presumptions in s 114 are the ones most often argued, and one illustration has a life of its own.
Section 114 illustration (g): the court may presume that evidence which could be and is not produced would, if produced, be unfavourable to the person who withholds it.

It is invoked whenever a party fails to call an available and material witness. It is a permissive presumption, not an automatic consequence, and the court will ask whether the witness was genuinely material and genuinely available before drawing anything from the omission.
Failing to call a witness whose evidence would merely repeat what is already proved does not attract the inference. The provision is about withheld evidence, not about incomplete evidence.

Confessions are admissions in criminal cases, and the Act treats them as a distinct class with their own conditions. A confession is irrelevant if it appears to have been caused by inducement, threat or promise proceeding from a person in authority and sufficient to give the accused grounds for supposing they would gain an advantage or avoid an evil.
This is one of the most heavily litigated parts of the Act and the case law is extensive. Read the sections themselves before any commentary, and be careful with older authority.

No cards or problems for this module yet. The single most useful exercise is to take a fact you would want to prove, and find the section that makes it relevant. Doing that ten times teaches the Act better than reading a chapter about it.

lessons.title: How a civil action is shaped
lessons.summary: Choosing the mode of commencement, pleading a case, and the interlocutory steps that dispose of most of them.

body.text: Most civil disputes are never tried. They are decided by a limitation point, a striking out, a summary judgment, or a settlement produced by one of those becoming likely. Procedure is where the outcome is usually determined, and treating it as the boring part is a mistake students make once.
The Rules of Court 2012 govern, and they unified what had been separate sets of rules for the High Court and the subordinate courts.
The first question on any set of facts is whether the claim is already time-barred, because if it is, nothing else matters.
Actions founded on contract or on tort must generally be brought within six years of the date on which the cause of action accrued; actions to recover land, within twelve.

Accrual is not the same as the wrongful act. In contract the cause of action accrues on breach; in tort it generally accrues when damage occurs, which may be much later. Getting accrual wrong is how a claim is filed a year out of time.
Two principal modes, and the choice is not stylistic.

items: Writ — where there is likely to be a substantial dispute of fact. Evidence is given orally and tested by cross-examination.
Originating summons — where the dispute is one of construction of a document or statute, or of law on essentially undisputed facts. Evidence is by affidavit.

body.text: Choosing wrongly is not usually fatal, since the court can order the proceedings to continue as if begun the other way, but it wastes time and costs and it signals inexperience.
A dispute about what a clause in a lease means, where nobody disagrees about what was signed, is an originating summons. A dispute about whether a representation was made at a meeting is a writ.
Pleadings define the issues. The statement of claim sets out the material facts the plaintiff relies on; the defence answers them; a reply may follow.
Plead material facts, not evidence and not law. A pleading states what happened, in the facts that give rise to the right claimed.

Two consequences follow and both are examined. A party is bound by their pleadings and cannot run a case at trial that was not pleaded. And an allegation not traversed in the defence is generally taken as admitted, so a bare denial of everything is not a defence and a silence is an admission.

Some matters must be pleaded specifically — fraud, misrepresentation, breach of trust, and any matter which if not pleaded would take the other side by surprise. Pleading fraud without particulars is worse than not pleading it.

sections.h: The interlocutory steps that end cases

items: Judgment in default, where the defendant fails to enter appearance or to serve a defence in time.
Summary judgment, where there is no defence with a real prospect of success and no other reason for a trial.
Striking out, where a pleading discloses no reasonable cause of action or defence, is scandalous or vexatious, or is an abuse of process.
Discovery, where each side must disclose the documents relevant to the matters in question — including the documents that hurt them.

body.text: Summary judgment and striking out are the two that decide the most cases, and the threshold for both is deliberately high: the court is depriving a party of a trial. The applicant must show the case is clear, and any genuinely triable issue defeats the application.

Do not confuse them. Striking out attacks the pleading on its face — assume the facts pleaded are true and ask whether they disclose a case. Summary judgment looks at the evidence and asks whether the defence is real.

A judgment is not money. Enforcement is a separate exercise with its own procedures — execution against goods, garnishment of debts owed to the judgment debtor, charging orders over land, and winding up or bankruptcy in the appropriate case. Advising a client that they have won is incomplete advice if the defendant has nothing.
Appeals run through the hierarchy under the Courts of Judicature Act 1964, with leave required at certain stages. Time limits for appealing are short and are strictly applied.

No cards or problems for this module yet. The exercise that teaches this fastest is to take a simple set of facts and write out the sequence: limitation, mode, pleading, the interlocutory application the other side would make, and what you would need to defeat it.

sections.h: A note about this module's reading

body.text: The reading list flags a genuine gap: no current Malaysian student text has been identified for administrative law, and the reference work is English. That matters more here than in most modules, because the Malaysian courts have taken a distinctive line on the central question of how far review may go.

Use the English text for the structure and the vocabulary, which travel well. Do not use it for the scope of review in Malaysia, which is different. Read the Malaysian judgments directly — this is the module where that is not optional advice.

sections.h: What judicial review is, and is not

body.text: Judicial review is the supervisory jurisdiction of the High Court over the exercise of public power. It is not an appeal. On an appeal the question is whether the decision was right; on review the traditional question is whether the decision was lawfully made.

It runs against public bodies exercising public functions, and the remedies are the prerogative orders — certiorari to quash, prohibition to forbid, mandamus to compel — along with declarations and injunctions. The procedure is by application for leave, then the substantive hearing.
Judicial review is commenced by an application for leave, and an applicant must be adversely affected by the decision complained of.
The standing requirement was for many years read narrowly, and the trend of the later authority has been to relax it. Check the current position rather than assuming either extreme.
The standard classification, which Malaysian courts use, comes from the GCHQ case and is the frame for almost every answer.
Illegality, irrationality, and procedural impropriety.
body.source: Council of Civil Service Unions v Minister for the Civil Service [1985] AC 374 (GCHQ)

items: Illegality — the decision-maker misdirected itself in law, acted beyond its powers, used a power for an improper purpose, took into account irrelevant considerations or ignored relevant ones, or fettered its own discretion.
Irrationality — the decision is so unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have come to it. This is the Wednesbury standard, and it is deliberately demanding.
Procedural impropriety — a failure to observe the procedure laid down, or a breach of natural justice: the right to be heard, and the rule against bias.

body.text: Natural justice is where the two Latin maxims from the foundations module do their work. Audi alteram partem requires that a person affected be heard; nemo judex in causa sua requires that the decision-maker have no interest in the outcome, and the test for bias is generally an objective one about apparent bias rather than proof of actual partiality.

Legitimate expectation sits alongside these: where a public body has promised a benefit or a procedure, or has consistently followed a practice, a person may be entitled to expect it to continue, or at least to be heard before it is withdrawn.

sections.h: How far the court may go

body.text: This is the question on which Malaysian administrative law departs from the orthodox English position, and it is the thing to know from this module if you know one thing.

The traditional view confines review to the decision-making process. The court quashes an unlawful decision and remits it; it does not substitute its own view of the merits, because the power was given to the decision-maker and not to the judge.

R Rama Chandran: on judicial review the court may in appropriate cases examine the substance or merits of a decision, and may grant relief that includes substituting its own decision rather than merely quashing and remitting.
body.source: R Rama Chandran v The Industrial Court of Malaysia [1997] 1 MLJ 145 (FC)

body.text: The reasoning is practical as well as doctrinal: remitting a matter to a tribunal that has already reached a conclusion can leave a successful applicant with nothing but delay. The decision has been applied, qualified and debated since, and the boundaries of when substitution is appropriate are not fixed.

Do not overstate it. Rama Chandran did not turn judicial review into an appeal, and later authority has been careful about its limits. Cite it for the proposition that merits review is available in appropriate cases, and then argue whether this is such a case.

Legislation sometimes provides that a decision shall be final, or shall not be questioned in any court. Whether such a clause defeats review is an old question with a settled direction of travel: the courts read ouster clauses narrowly, and a decision made outside jurisdiction is treated as no decision at all and therefore not protected.

In Malaysia this connects to the constitutional material in the legal system module. The Federal Court's reasoning in Semenyih Jaya and Indira Gandhi treats judicial power and judicial review as part of the basic structure, which places a limit on how far any clause — or any amendment — can exclude the courts.
Judicial review of administrative action is inherent in the civil courts and forms part of the basic structure of the Constitution.
body.source: Indira Gandhi a/p Mutho v Pengarah Jabatan Agama Islam Perak [2018] 1 MLJ 545 (FC)

quiz.q: What are the three grounds of judicial review?
options: Ultra vires, bias, error of fact
Error of law, error of fact, bad faith
quiz.why: Proportionality is argued as a fourth, and its status should be checked rather than assumed.

quiz.q: What is the irrationality standard?
options: So unreasonable that no reasonable authority could have come to it
quiz.why: The Wednesbury standard, and it is deliberately hard to satisfy.

quiz.q: What must an applicant for judicial review show at the threshold?
options: Leave, and that he is adversely affected by the decision
An arguable error of law only
quiz.why: Both are threshold requirements before the merits are reached.

options: That the court may in appropriate cases examine substance and substitute its own decision
That judicial review is an appeal

quiz.q: Why can an ouster clause not exclude judicial review altogether?
options: Judicial review of administrative action is inherent in the civil courts and part of the basic structure
Ouster clauses are void for uncertainty
Parliament never intends to oust review
The Rules of Court override statute
quiz.why: And an ouster clause is construed narrowly in any event.

lessons.title: How legal reasoning is actually done
lessons.summary: Rules and standards, reasoning by analogy, and why the answer is often genuinely open without being arbitrary.

body.text: Everything up to here has taught you rules. This module asks a different question: what kind of thinking is legal reasoning, and why does it so often produce disagreement between competent lawyers reading the same materials?

The answer is not that one side is incompetent or dishonest. It is that the materials genuinely underdetermine the outcome more often than a textbook's confident prose suggests, and knowing where that happens is what separates an argument from a recitation.
Legal directives come in two shapes, and the choice between them is a real design decision with costs on both sides.

items: A rule specifies its trigger in advance: drive no faster than 90 km/h. It is predictable, cheap to apply, and will sometimes produce a result nobody wanted — the ambulance, the empty road at 3am.
A standard states the goal and leaves application open: drive at a reasonable speed for the conditions. It fits every case and tells you nothing until a court has ruled.

body.text: Rules buy predictability at the cost of occasionally getting the individual case wrong. Standards buy accuracy in the individual case at the cost of predictability.

Noticing which one you are dealing with tells you what kind of argument will work. Against a rule you argue that the trigger is not satisfied, or that this is not a case the rule was meant to reach. Against a standard you argue the factors.

Section 300(c) of the Penal Code is close to a rule: intention to inflict the injury, and objective sufficiency to cause death. The reasonable person standard in negligence is a standard. The kind of argument that works against each is different.

Precedent works by analogy, and analogy is not a mechanical operation. Two cases are never identical, so the question is always whether they are alike in the respects that matter — and what matters is decided by the rule you take the earlier case to stand for.

That is why the argument about the level of generality at which a ratio is stated, from the precedent lesson, is not a technicality. State it narrowly and the earlier case is distinguishable; state it broadly and it governs. Both statements can be honestly defended from the same judgment.

This is not licence to say precedent means whatever you want. The range of defensible statements is real but bounded, and an argument outside it will simply lose. The skill is knowing where the edges are.

Rules are made of words, and words have a settled core and an uncertain edge. Hart's example is a rule prohibiting vehicles in a park: a car is plainly within it, a bicycle is arguable, and a war memorial tank on a plinth is the sort of case that makes the point.
Legal language has a core of settled meaning and a penumbra of doubt. Most cases are decided in the core and never litigated; the cases you read are disproportionately from the penumbra.
body.source: Hart, on the open texture of legal language

body.text: This explains something about your reading that is otherwise disorienting. The law reports contain the hard cases, because the easy ones settle or never start. Reading only reported cases gives a systematically distorted impression of how indeterminate the law is.
Two positions worth being able to state, because arguments about judicial decision-making usually reduce to a version of them.

Formalism holds that legal outcomes follow from legal materials — the rules, applied to the facts, give the answer, and the judge's role is to find it. Realism holds that outcomes are substantially driven by other factors, and the legal reasoning is a justification constructed afterwards.

Neither extreme survives contact with practice. Most cases really are determined by the materials; some really are not, and in those the judge is choosing. The useful question is not which camp is right but which kind of case you are in, because it decides whether your best argument is doctrinal or consequential.
Do not deploy realism as a way of avoiding doctrine. An answer that says the judge will decide as they please is not a legal argument, and it is wrong about the great majority of cases.

No cards or problems for this module yet. The exercise that pays here is to take a case you have already briefed and write the ratio twice — once as narrowly as the judgment honestly allows, once as broadly. Then say which side would argue for which, and why. That is the whole module in one page.

quiz.q: What is the trade-off between a rule and a standard?
options: Rules buy predictability at the cost of occasionally getting the case wrong; standards buy accuracy at the cost of predictability
Rules are statutory and standards are judicial
quiz.why: Which to prefer is a design question, and the answer depends on what the provision is for.

quiz.q: What is the 'penumbra of doubt'?
options: The area where a term's application is genuinely uncertain
A rule that has been overruled
A statutory ambiguity resolved by definition
quiz.why: Most cases are decided in the core and never litigated; the ones you read come disproportionately from the penumbra.

quiz.q: What is wrong with deploying legal realism to say the judge will decide as they please?
options: It is not a legal argument, and it is wrong about how most cases are decided
It is only true of appellate courts
Judges are not permitted to consider policy
quiz.why: The range of defensible positions is real but bounded.

quiz.why: You can state a ratio at more than one level of generality, but not at any level you like.

lessons.title: Reading a statute
lessons.summary: Malaysia has made the purposive approach statutory, which changes what the traditional rules are for.

sections.h: The provision that changes the subject

body.text: Most treatments of statutory interpretation begin with three common law rules — literal, golden and mischief — and work towards the purposive approach as a modern development. In Malaysia that ordering is misleading, because the purposive approach is not a judicial preference. It is enacted.

In the interpretation of a provision of an Act, a construction that would promote the purpose or object underlying the Act shall be preferred to a construction that would not promote that purpose or object.

Read that carefully: shall be preferred. It is a direction to the court, not an option among approaches. Any answer on Malaysian statutory interpretation that works through the three common law rules and reaches purposive construction as a possible modern alternative has the structure backwards.
This is the single most common error in this module, and it comes directly from using English or older textbooks. Start from s 17A.

sections.h: What the traditional rules are still for

body.text: They are not obsolete. They describe recurring moves within a purposive framework rather than competing methods.

items: The literal approach — give the words their ordinary meaning. Still the starting point: purpose does not licence ignoring the text, and a construction the words cannot bear is not available however desirable.

The golden rule — depart from the literal meaning where it produces an absurdity. Now largely subsumed, since an absurd result is strong evidence that a construction does not promote the Act's purpose.

The mischief rule — ask what defect in the previous law the Act was passed to remedy. This is the closest ancestor of s 17A and remains a good way to identify the purpose the section directs you to serve.

body.text: So the structure of a good answer is: what do the words naturally mean; what is the purpose of the Act; and does the natural meaning promote it. Where the answer to the last is no, s 17A tells you which construction to prefer.

Internal aids are parts of the Act itself: the long title, the preamble where there is one, headings, marginal notes, the interpretation section, provisos, explanations and schedules. The interpretation section is the one students skip and should not — a defined term means what the Act says it means, whatever it means elsewhere.

External aids sit outside the Act: dictionaries, earlier legislation on the same subject, international conventions the Act implements, and parliamentary material. The use of Hansard is the contested one, and you should check the current Malaysian position rather than assuming the English rule applies.
Words in the singular include the plural and words in the plural include the singular, unless a contrary intention appears.

That looks trivial and is not. It is the provision, applied to “parent” in Article 12(4), that decided the conversion question in Indira Gandhi — a rule of interpretation carrying a constitutional case.
Presumptions are default positions that the legislature is taken to have intended unless it says otherwise.

items: Against retrospective operation, particularly for provisions affecting substantive rights.
Against ousting the jurisdiction of the courts.
In favour of a mental element in a criminal offence, so that strict liability is not lightly inferred.
That penal provisions are construed strictly, and ambiguity resolved in favour of the accused.

body.text: The linguistic canons are narrower tools. Ejusdem generis: general words following a list of specific items are read as limited to the same class. Noscitur a sociis: a word takes colour from its neighbours. Expressio unius est exclusio alterius: expressing one thing implies the exclusion of others — the weakest of the three, and easily over-applied.
A provision applying to “cars, vans, lorries and other vehicles” will, under ejusdem generis, probably not reach a bicycle: the specific items share a class, and the general words are read within it.

A constitution is not an ordinary statute and is not read like one. The Malaysian courts have repeatedly said that fundamental liberties are to be construed generously and not with the narrowness appropriate to a penal provision, and that a constitution should be read as a living document rather than as a conveyance.

The Eleventh Schedule applies certain provisions of the Interpretation Acts to the Constitution, which is how the singular-includes-plural rule reached Article 12(4). But the interpretive posture is different, and importing the strict approach appropriate to a taxing statute into Part II is an error.

No cards or problems for this module yet. Read s 17A itself — it is one sentence — and then take any section you have already worked with and construct the argument both ways: the literal reading, the purposive reading, and which s 17A directs you to prefer.
